items.title: I can define mental wellbeing using precise psychological language
items.what: Mental wellbeing is an individual's psychological state, including their ability to think, process information, and regulate emotions. It is not simply the absence of mental illness.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to define mental wellbeing accurately; using vague language such as 'feeling happy' will not attract marks.
items.example: A student who is managing exam stress effectively, processing information clearly in class, and regulating frustration when things go wrong is demonstrating good mental wellbeing — even if they feel some anxiety.

subtopic.name: Protective Factors Overview
subtopic.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They are organised within the biopsychosocial framework as biological, psychological, and social influences that interact and are best used together.
subtopic.why: Understanding what protective factors are — and what they are not — helps students apply the concept accurately in exam contexts, particularly distinguishing them from evidence-based treatments for mental health disorders.

items.title: I can define protective factors and explain their two functions
items.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They function in two ways: by reducing the risk of low mental wellbeing or mental health disorders, and by increasing the likelihood of high mental wellbeing.
items.why: Knowing both functions prevents students from describing protective factors as only reducing risk — they also actively promote positive states.
items.example: Regular adequate sleep (a biological protective factor) both reduces the risk of developing depression and actively promotes positive mood, cognitive clarity, and emotional regulation.

subtopic.name: Protective Factors Overview
subtopic.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They are organised within the biopsychosocial framework as biological, psychological, and social influences that interact and are best used together.
subtopic.why: Understanding what protective factors are — and what they are not — helps students apply the concept accurately in exam contexts, particularly distinguishing them from evidence-based treatments for mental health disorders.

items.title: I can explain why protective factors do not guarantee high mental wellbeing
items.what: Protective factors may improve mental wellbeing but do not guarantee it. For some individuals experiencing low mental wellbeing, further interventions and treatments may be required beyond day-to-day protective factors.
items.why: This distinction is important for evaluating claims in extended response and data analysis questions — students must avoid overstating the effectiveness of protective factors.
items.example: A person who eats well, sleeps adequately, and has strong social support may still develop a mental health disorder; protective factors reduce risk but cannot eliminate it entirely.

subtopic.name: Protective Factors Overview
subtopic.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They are organised within the biopsychosocial framework as biological, psychological, and social influences that interact and are best used together.
subtopic.why: Understanding what protective factors are — and what they are not — helps students apply the concept accurately in exam contexts, particularly distinguishing them from evidence-based treatments for mental health disorders.

items.title: I can distinguish protective factors from evidence-based interventions
items.what: Protective factors are tools used in day-to-day life to maintain or promote mental wellbeing. Evidence-based interventions, such as systematic desensitisation or CBT delivered by a clinician, are designed to treat an existing mental health condition.
items.why: VCE exam questions may present scenarios requiring students to correctly identify whether a strategy is a protective factor or a clinical intervention — conflating the two is a common error.
items.example: Practicing mindfulness meditation daily to maintain calm is a protective factor. A structured 12-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy program delivered by a psychologist to treat recurrent depression is an evidence-based intervention.

subtopic.name: Protective Factors Overview
subtopic.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They are organised within the biopsychosocial framework as biological, psychological, and social influences that interact and are best used together.
subtopic.why: Understanding what protective factors are — and what they are not — helps students apply the concept accurately in exam contexts, particularly distinguishing them from evidence-based treatments for mental health disorders.

items.title: I can apply the biopsychosocial approach to protective factors by explaining why a combination is most effective
items.what: The biopsychosocial model holds that biological, psychological, and social influences interact with each other and are equally important. Applying this to protective factors means a combination across all three domains is likely to be more effective than relying on any single factor.
items.why: Exam scenarios frequently ask students to suggest a biopsychosocial approach to maintaining wellbeing; identifying one factor from each domain and explaining their interaction is required for higher-mark responses.
items.example: For a VCE student stressed about exams, using all three domains together — adequate sleep (biological), mindfulness meditation (psychological), and support from friends and family (social) — is more effective than sleep alone.

subtopic.name: Protective Factors Overview
subtopic.what: Protective factors are influences that enable an individual to promote and maintain high levels of mental wellbeing. They are organised within the biopsychosocial framework as biological, psychological, and social influences that interact and are best used together.
subtopic.why: Understanding what protective factors are — and what they are not — helps students apply the concept accurately in exam contexts, particularly distinguishing them from evidence-based treatments for mental health disorders.

items.title: I can define adequate nutrition and hydration as a biological protective factor
items.what: Adequate nutrition and hydration refers to when the type and amount of food and drink an individual consumes meets their physical needs, including sufficient water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
items.why: A precise definition is required in short-answer responses; students who only refer to 'eating healthily' without specifying what adequate means risk losing marks.
items.example: An individual who consumes approximately 2–3 litres of water per day, eats a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, legumes, and nuts, and avoids excess processed foods is demonstrating adequate nutrition and hydration.

subtopic.name: Biological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Biological protective factors are influences that stem from an individual's brain and body that can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two biological protective factors in this study design are adequate nutrition and hydration, and sleep.
subtopic.why: Both nutrition and sleep have well-documented bidirectional relationships with mental wellbeing, meaning students must be able to explain causation in both directions — not just that good biology supports good mental health, but that poor mental health can impair biological functioning.

items.title: I can compare a Mediterranean-style diet with a Western-style diet in terms of mental wellbeing outcomes
items.what: Research suggests a Mediterranean-style diet — high in unprocessed foods such as fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and seeds — is associated with reduced risk of mental health disorders including depression and anxiety. A Western-style diet — high in processed foods, added sugar, salt, saturated fats, and alcohol — is associated with increased risk.
items.why: Exam questions may present a dietary scenario and ask students to evaluate the mental wellbeing implications; knowing the specific features of each diet pattern allows a precise answer.
items.example: A person who replaces daily fast food and sugary drinks with Mediterranean-style meals of grilled fish, salad, legumes, and water may reduce their risk of developing depression, according to research by Firth et al. (2020).

subtopic.name: Biological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Biological protective factors are influences that stem from an individual's brain and body that can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two biological protective factors in this study design are adequate nutrition and hydration, and sleep.
subtopic.why: Both nutrition and sleep have well-documented bidirectional relationships with mental wellbeing, meaning students must be able to explain causation in both directions — not just that good biology supports good mental health, but that poor mental health can impair biological functioning.

items.title: I can explain the bidirectional relationship between adequate nutrition and hydration and mental wellbeing
items.what: The relationship between adequate nutrition and hydration and mental wellbeing is bidirectional: adequate nutrition can protect against conditions such as depression, but depression can also impair appetite and motivation to eat, making it more difficult for a person with depression to maintain adequate nutrition.
items.why: The bidirectional nature of this relationship is explicitly named in the curriculum content and is likely to appear in extended response questions that ask students to explain complexity or limitations.
items.example: A person experiencing depression may find it difficult to cook or eat regularly, leading to nutritional deficiency, which in turn worsens depressive symptoms — illustrating how the relationship operates in both directions.

subtopic.name: Biological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Biological protective factors are influences that stem from an individual's brain and body that can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two biological protective factors in this study design are adequate nutrition and hydration, and sleep.
subtopic.why: Both nutrition and sleep have well-documented bidirectional relationships with mental wellbeing, meaning students must be able to explain causation in both directions — not just that good biology supports good mental health, but that poor mental health can impair biological functioning.

items.title: I can explain why sleep is a biological protective factor for mental wellbeing
items.what: Sleep is a regular, naturally occurring altered state of consciousness involving loss of awareness and disengagement from internal and external stimuli. Adequate sleep is linked to reduced likelihood of mental health disorders and promotes mental wellbeing, acting as a protective factor.
items.why: Students must be able to define sleep precisely (as previously studied) and connect it to mental wellbeing outcomes — simply stating 'sleep is good for you' is insufficient at VCE level.
items.example: Research by Scott et al. (2017) suggests a link between poor sleep quality, sleep deprivation, and increased risk of mental illness — meaning a student who maintains consistent, quality sleep is reducing this risk.

subtopic.name: Biological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Biological protective factors are influences that stem from an individual's brain and body that can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two biological protective factors in this study design are adequate nutrition and hydration, and sleep.
subtopic.why: Both nutrition and sleep have well-documented bidirectional relationships with mental wellbeing, meaning students must be able to explain causation in both directions — not just that good biology supports good mental health, but that poor mental health can impair biological functioning.

items.title: I can explain the bidirectional relationship between sleep and mental wellbeing
items.what: Sleep and mental wellbeing have a bidirectional relationship: adequate sleep promotes mental wellbeing, but poor mental wellbeing (such as anxiety or depression) can in turn impair sleep quality and duration.
items.why: Bidirectionality is a key concept that distinguishes higher-level responses from those that only describe one direction of causation; it also reflects the complexity of real psychological phenomena.
items.example: A person experiencing high anxiety may find it difficult to fall asleep due to rumination, resulting in sleep deprivation, which then worsens their anxiety the following day — a reinforcing cycle in both directions.

subtopic.name: Biological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Biological protective factors are influences that stem from an individual's brain and body that can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two biological protective factors in this study design are adequate nutrition and hydration, and sleep.
subtopic.why: Both nutrition and sleep have well-documented bidirectional relationships with mental wellbeing, meaning students must be able to explain causation in both directions — not just that good biology supports good mental health, but that poor mental health can impair biological functioning.

items.title: I can define psychological protective factors
items.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to an individual's mental processes — their thoughts, feelings, and behaviours — that can maintain and promote mental wellbeing.
items.why: Clearly distinguishing psychological protective factors from biological and social ones is necessary for accurately categorising strategies in both short-answer and extended response questions.
items.example: Choosing to challenge a negative thought pattern about an upcoming exam (a cognitive process) is a psychological protective factor, whereas getting adequate sleep the night before is biological.

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can define cognitive behavioural strategies and identify their cognitive and behavioural components
items.what: Cognitive behavioural strategies are techniques that use features of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) — particularly recognising and changing dysfunctional thought and behavioural patterns. The cognitive component involves identifying and replacing dysfunctional thoughts; the behavioural component involves identifying and replacing dysfunctional behaviours.
items.why: Students must distinguish the cognitive and behavioural components separately, as exam questions may ask students to identify which component a given example illustrates.
items.example: A student who identifies the thought 'I will definitely fail this exam' as dysfunctional (cognitive component) and then replaces it with 'I have studied consistently and am likely to pass' is using the cognitive component of CBT strategies.

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can apply cognitive behavioural strategies to a scenario by identifying dysfunctional thoughts and behaviours and their replacements
items.what: Applying CBT strategies means identifying a specific dysfunctional thought or behaviour in a given scenario, explaining why it is dysfunctional, and describing a functional replacement thought or behaviour.
items.why: Exam questions routinely present a character in a stressful situation and ask students to apply a protective factor — CBT strategies require a structured, step-by-step application rather than a vague statement.
items.example: Pim, whose grandfather has been diagnosed with cancer, might have the dysfunctional thought 'this is hopeless and nothing will get better.' A CBT strategy would involve identifying this as dysfunctional, and replacing it with 'the treatment is likely to be successful, and my family and I can support each other through this.'

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can define mindfulness meditation and identify its key features
items.what: Mindfulness meditation is the practice of focusing attention on the present moment — including current feelings, thoughts, and surroundings — while observing this experience with kindness and without judgement. It is typically practised by sitting comfortably and directing attention to sensory experience.
items.why: Students must define mindfulness meditation precisely; a common error is conflating it with general relaxation or with CBT strategies — each has a distinct definition.
items.example: A person sitting quietly for ten minutes, noticing the sensation of breathing, acknowledging anxious thoughts about tomorrow without judging them, and returning attention to the breath is practising mindfulness meditation.

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can outline the mental wellbeing benefits of mindfulness meditation supported by research
items.what: Research (Eberth et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012) suggests mindfulness meditation can improve emotional reactivity, reduce rumination (repeatedly considering negative thoughts), reduce stress, and improve memory.
items.why: Being able to name specific benefits with research support strengthens exam responses, particularly in questions that ask students to explain how mindfulness meditation promotes mental wellbeing.
items.example: A person who ruminates over a social conflict may use daily mindfulness meditation to reduce the frequency and intensity of these recurring negative thoughts, as supported by Davis et al. (2012).

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can explain why mindfulness meditation may be particularly useful for individuals experiencing anxiety
items.what: Anxiety is characterised by excessive worry about future events. Because mindfulness meditation redirects attention to the present moment, it can help individuals with anxiety disengage from future-focused worry and reduce its impact on wellbeing.
items.why: Linking mindfulness specifically to anxiety connects two different parts of the study design and demonstrates the capacity for higher-level integration that is rewarded in extended responses.
items.example: A student anxious about an upcoming assessment who practises mindfulness meditation is trained to notice worry thoughts about the exam as they arise, observe them without acting on them, and return attention to the present — interrupting the cycle of anxious rumination.

subtopic.name: Psychological Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Psychological protective factors are influences that relate to mental processes and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The two psychological protective factors in this study design are cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation.
subtopic.why: These factors are central to the VCE study design and frequently appear in exam scenarios requiring students to explain or apply a specific psychological strategy to a character's situation.

items.title: I can define social protective factors and give an example
items.what: Social protective factors are influences that exist in an individual's social environment that can maintain and promote mental wellbeing. The primary example in this study design is support.
items.why: Exam questions may ask students to identify or classify a protective factor; being able to clearly define what makes a factor 'social' avoids the common error of labelling psychological strategies as social ones.
items.example: Attending a community sporting club where a student feels a sense of belonging is a social protective factor — the influence originates in their external social environment, not in their biology or individual thought processes.

subtopic.name: Social Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Social protective factors are influences that exist in an individual's social environment and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The key social protective factor in this study design is support from family, friends, and community that is authentic and energising.
subtopic.why: Students must understand what makes support genuinely protective — its quality and authenticity matter, not just its presence — and be able to distinguish examples of support from each of the three sources (family, friends, community).

items.title: I can define support as a social protective factor and explain what makes it authentic and energising
items.what: Support refers to genuine and effective assistance provided by family, friends, and community. For support to function as a protective factor, it must be authentic and energising — meaning it genuinely aims to promote wellbeing, creates an environment likely to improve mental wellbeing, and uses legitimate and effective advice.
items.why: The study design specifies that support must be authentic and energising; generic support that is dismissive or unhelpful would not qualify as a protective factor and may not attract marks in a precise exam answer.
items.example: A friend who listens actively, validates feelings, and suggests realistic coping strategies when someone is stressed is providing authentic and energising support. A friend who dismisses concerns with 'just stop worrying' is not.

subtopic.name: Social Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Social protective factors are influences that exist in an individual's social environment and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The key social protective factor in this study design is support from family, friends, and community that is authentic and energising.
subtopic.why: Students must understand what makes support genuinely protective — its quality and authenticity matter, not just its presence — and be able to distinguish examples of support from each of the three sources (family, friends, community).

items.title: I can identify and explain examples of support from family, friends, and community
items.what: Family support includes unconditional love, regular emotional catch-ups, and encouragement to avoid unhealthy behaviours. Friend support includes fun and energising experiences, intimacy, and distraction from difficult emotions. Community support includes opportunities for interaction and bonding, a sense of belonging, facilities for psychological or practical assistance, and opportunities for personal growth.
items.why: Exam scenarios often specify the source of support (e.g., 'Cloe's friend group') and ask students to explain how that specific type of support promotes wellbeing — students who can draw on examples from each category answer more specifically.
items.example: When Pim's grandfather is ill, family support might involve regular conversations where family members share feelings openly, providing a familiar and stable sense of belonging during uncertainty.

subtopic.name: Social Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Social protective factors are influences that exist in an individual's social environment and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The key social protective factor in this study design is support from family, friends, and community that is authentic and energising.
subtopic.why: Students must understand what makes support genuinely protective — its quality and authenticity matter, not just its presence — and be able to distinguish examples of support from each of the three sources (family, friends, community).

items.title: I can evaluate the limitations of social support as a standalone protective factor
items.what: While social support is a valuable protective factor, it does not guarantee high mental wellbeing on its own. A single protective factor — even strong social support — may be insufficient if other biological and psychological factors are not also addressed.
items.why: A common exam question asks students to evaluate whether a character's belief that one protective factor is enough is accurate; correctly identifying limitations and linking back to the biopsychosocial model is required for full marks.
items.example: Cloe may believe her supportive friend group means she will always have high mental wellbeing, but without also attending to sleep, nutrition, and psychological strategies, her wellbeing could still be at risk during major stressors.

subtopic.name: Social Protective Factors
subtopic.what: Social protective factors are influences that exist in an individual's social environment and can maintain or promote mental wellbeing. The key social protective factor in this study design is support from family, friends, and community that is authentic and energising.
subtopic.why: Students must understand what makes support genuinely protective — its quality and authenticity matter, not just its presence — and be able to distinguish examples of support from each of the three sources (family, friends, community).

items.title: I can define determinants of wellbeing
items.what: Determinants of wellbeing are factors that influence wellbeing on individual and community levels. They range from physical environment factors to economic, social, and cultural factors.
items.why: Students need to distinguish 'determinants of wellbeing' from 'protective factors' — determinants is a broader term that includes cultural factors integral to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander wellbeing.
items.example: Access to safe housing is a social determinant of wellbeing; connection to Country is a cultural determinant of wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

subtopic.name: Cultural Determinants of Wellbeing
subtopic.what: Cultural determinants of wellbeing are factors related to culture that influence wellbeing on both individual and community levels. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses identity, values, tradition, and connection across past, present, and future generations.
subtopic.why: Understanding the historical context of why cultural determinants are integral — including the impact of colonisation and the Stolen Generations — is necessary to answer questions about this topic with cultural respect and analytical depth.

items.title: I can explain what culture means for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.what: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses a strong sense of identity, values, tradition, and connection between the past, present, and future that drives behaviour and beliefs. The Lowitja Institute describes it as providing the life-giving values from which individuals, families, and communities draw strength, resilience, and empowerment.
items.why: This definition reflects a specifically First Nations conceptualisation of culture that differs from everyday uses of the word; students who use only a generic definition will not fully address the question.
items.example: For a Gunditjmara elder, culture might mean transmitting knowledge of Country to younger family members through storytelling and ceremony — an act that simultaneously connects the past, present, and future.

subtopic.name: Cultural Determinants of Wellbeing
subtopic.what: Cultural determinants of wellbeing are factors related to culture that influence wellbeing on both individual and community levels. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses identity, values, tradition, and connection across past, present, and future generations.
subtopic.why: Understanding the historical context of why cultural determinants are integral — including the impact of colonisation and the Stolen Generations — is necessary to answer questions about this topic with cultural respect and analytical depth.

items.title: I can explain why cultural determinants are considered protective factors for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.what: Cultural determinants — such as cultural continuity and self-determination — act as protective factors because cultural connectedness and knowledge are vital components of health and wellbeing. Engaging with culture provides strength, resilience, and empowerment that promote and maintain wellbeing.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to link cultural determinants to the concept of protective factors from lesson 10A — making this connection explicitly demonstrates integration across the study design.
items.example: A young Wiradjuri person who participates in community language programs and cultural events may experience increased cultural identity and sense of belonging, which promotes mental wellbeing in the same way that social support does under the biopsychosocial model.

subtopic.name: Cultural Determinants of Wellbeing
subtopic.what: Cultural determinants of wellbeing are factors related to culture that influence wellbeing on both individual and community levels. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses identity, values, tradition, and connection across past, present, and future generations.
subtopic.why: Understanding the historical context of why cultural determinants are integral — including the impact of colonisation and the Stolen Generations — is necessary to answer questions about this topic with cultural respect and analytical depth.

items.title: I can explain the historical context of why cultural determinants are particularly important for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.what: Colonial policies from the early 1900s through to the 1970s included forced family separations and punishment for cultural practices, affecting those known as the Stolen Generations. The resulting intergenerational trauma means that cultural continuity and self-determination are especially important for healing and re-establishing wellbeing in affected communities.
items.why: Questions asking students to explain why cultural determinants are integral — not just what they are — require this historical context. Omitting it produces a superficial answer.
items.example: A descendant of the Stolen Generations who has limited knowledge of their ancestral language or traditions may experience a diminished sense of cultural identity; participation in language reclamation programs can begin to restore this connection and support wellbeing.

subtopic.name: Cultural Determinants of Wellbeing
subtopic.what: Cultural determinants of wellbeing are factors related to culture that influence wellbeing on both individual and community levels. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses identity, values, tradition, and connection across past, present, and future generations.
subtopic.why: Understanding the historical context of why cultural determinants are integral — including the impact of colonisation and the Stolen Generations — is necessary to answer questions about this topic with cultural respect and analytical depth.

items.title: I can identify a range of cultural determinants of wellbeing beyond cultural continuity and self-determination
items.what: While the study design focuses on cultural continuity and self-determination, a broader range of cultural determinants exists, including Indigenous language, connection to Country, family and kinship, cultural expression, and Indigenous beliefs and knowledge.
items.why: Awareness of the broader range of cultural determinants allows students to demonstrate depth and apply the concept to novel scenarios in extended responses and media analysis tasks.
items.example: An Aboriginal student who participates in a Songlines workshop at school is engaging with connection to Country and Indigenous beliefs and knowledge — cultural determinants that sit alongside but are distinct from the two specifically assessed in this study design.

subtopic.name: Cultural Determinants of Wellbeing
subtopic.what: Cultural determinants of wellbeing are factors related to culture that influence wellbeing on both individual and community levels. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culture encompasses identity, values, tradition, and connection across past, present, and future generations.
subtopic.why: Understanding the historical context of why cultural determinants are integral — including the impact of colonisation and the Stolen Generations — is necessary to answer questions about this topic with cultural respect and analytical depth.

items.title: I can define cultural continuity precisely
items.what: Cultural continuity is the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. The key distinction is that it occurs across generations — not merely from person to person — and involves both transmission and active ongoing practice.
items.why: A common exam error is defining cultural continuity as passing culture 'from person to person'; the correct definition specifies generation to generation, and this distinction is tested directly in the study design questions.
items.example: An Arrernte grandmother teaching her grandchildren traditional sand drawing and the stories associated with each symbol is enacting cultural continuity — the knowledge passes across a generational line and is actively practised.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can identify how cultural continuity can be practised and maintained
items.what: Cultural continuity can be maintained through a wide range of cultural practices, including arts, crafts, music, dance, theatre, storytelling, written language, spoken language, food preparation, and ceremony.
items.why: Exam and SAC questions often ask students to suggest how cultural continuity can be achieved; being able to give a range of specific examples across different modes of cultural expression demonstrates thorough understanding.
items.example: A secondary school that incorporates an Aboriginal language program taught by an Elder in Residence is supporting cultural continuity by enabling young students to learn their mother tongue in a structured educational setting.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can explain how disruption to cultural continuity has affected the wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.what: Colonial assimilation and protection policies that separated First Nations people from their families and punished them for speaking their languages or practising their culture disrupted cultural continuity from the early 1900s through the 1970s. The resulting intergenerational trauma means many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are still working towards healing and re-establishing cultural identity and wellbeing.
items.why: Explaining disruption to cultural continuity is necessary for understanding why it is described as 'integral' to wellbeing — not merely helpful, but essential for healing historical harm.
items.example: A person whose grandparents were part of the Stolen Generations and were prevented from speaking their language may have limited access to their ancestral tongue; language reclamation programs address this specific gap in cultural continuity.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can define self-determination precisely using the United Nations definition
items.what: Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference. It applies to nations as a whole and recognises that First Nations peoples have the right to make decisions about matters that affect them.
items.why: The precise definition matters for exam questions; a common error is defining self-determination as individuals making their own personal decisions, which conflates it with autonomy at the personal level rather than the community and national level.
items.example: The APY Lands Traditional Owners closing access to their region in early March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 spread — before the Australian government acted — is an example of community-level self-determination protecting community wellbeing.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can identify specific endeavours through which self-determination is enacted
items.what: Self-determination can be enacted through Aboriginal community-controlled organisations, partnerships between communities and governments or non-government organisations, and constitutional recognition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples as the First Nations of Australia.
items.why: Exam questions ask students to identify specific examples of self-determination rather than speak in generalities; knowing at least three concrete endeavours allows precise, mark-attracting answers.
items.example: An Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (ACCHO) that designs and delivers health services according to the needs and values of its community is a direct enactment of self-determination.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can explain why self-determination is integral to the maintenance of wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.what: Self-determination is integral to wellbeing because autonomy and the ability to govern one's own life contribute fundamentally to an individual's and community's sense of control. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples specifically, self-determination enables communities to protect what is most important to them and to make decisions that reflect their own values, rather than having decisions imposed externally.
items.why: Questions asking why self-determination is integral — not just what it is — require a deeper explanation connecting autonomy to wellbeing outcomes; this level of reasoning is expected in 2-mark and extended response questions.
items.example: When Indigenous communities were able to implement their own COVID-19 restrictions and produce educational materials in their own languages, this exercise of self-determination also supported mental wellbeing by reinforcing community agency, identity, and collective efficacy.

subtopic.name: Cultural Continuity and Self-Determination
subtopic.what: Cultural continuity refers to the passing down and active practice of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values from generation to generation. Self-determination refers to the rights of all peoples to freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without outside interference.
subtopic.why: These two cultural determinants are explicitly named in the VCE study design and are the focus of exam questions that ask students to define, apply, and compare them in both abstract and scenario-based contexts.

items.title: I can compare cultural continuity and self-determination as two distinct but related cultural determinants of wellbeing
items.what: Cultural continuity focuses on the preservation and intergenerational transmission of cultural knowledge, traditions, and values. Self-determination focuses on the rights and capacity of peoples to govern their own economic, social, and cultural development. Both are cultural determinants that promote wellbeing, but cultural continuity operates primarily through identity and belonging, while self-determination operates through autonomy and community agency.
items.why: SAC and exam questions explicitly ask students to compare these two determinants; students who can clearly articulate how they are related but distinct will produce higher-quality responses than those who treat them as interchangeable.
items.example: A community language program demonstrates cultural continuity by transmitting language knowledge across generations. The fact that the program is designed and run by community members rather than government officials is an act of self-determination — the same activity can reflect both determinants simultaneously.
